units.source_en: They’re popular among space geeks, and they have for decades been the main pursuit of the National Space Society.
But unless partial gravity is a showstopper, we don’t see rotating space stations as a settlement priority for a long time.

paragraphs.source_en: Many of the arguments made for space stations have their historical origins during a particular period of the 1970s when it appeared that environmental degradation was going to cause imminent worldwide famines, and when the price of space launch appeared to be falling rapidly. Also, renewable tech that we take for granted, like cheap photovoltaics, massive wind turbines, and advanced battery storage, were still decades away. If you combine all those constraints—resource calamity in the extreme short term, space access very cheap, and no other options—there might maybe have been a case for huge solar-power-collecting space stations with factories and artificial human habitats. But the widespread famines never came,[*] renewables got cheap, and space travel has remained relatively costly, even accounting for recent changes.
